cards.q: Why does `println!` have an exclamation mark?
cards.a:
It is a macro, so it can take a format string and any number of arguments

The `!` means a macro call: macros can take a format string and a varying number of arguments, checked at compile time. Ordinary functions always take a fixed list of parameters.
cards.lessonTitle: Rust and Cargo: Your First Program

cards.q: What does `cargo check` do?
cards.a:
Type-checks the project without producing a program, faster than a build

`cargo check` only checks the code, so it is quicker than `cargo build`; the optimised build is `cargo build --release`.
cards.lessonTitle: Rust and Cargo: Your First Program

cards.q: What does `println!("{x:>5}")` print when x is 42?
cards.a:
42 right-aligned in 5 characters: "   42"

`>` aligns right within the given width, so the padding goes on the left; `<` would align left.
cards.lessonTitle: Rust and Cargo: Your First Program

cards.q: What is the difference between shadowing and `mut`?
cards.a:
`mut` lets one variable change; shadowing makes a new variable, possibly of another type

A new `let` with the same name declares a fresh variable, so its type may differ; `mut` lets the same variable take new values of the same type.

cards.q: Why does `let y: i64 = x;` not compile when `x` is an `i32`?
cards.a:
Rust never converts numbers implicitly; write `x.into()` or `i64::from(x)`

Every `i32` fits in an `i64`, but Rust still wants the conversion written out; `into()` and `from()` do it losslessly.

cards.q: In a debug build, what happens when a `u8` holding 255 has 1 added with `+`?
cards.a:
The program panics

Debug builds check for overflow; use wrapping_add, saturating_add or checked_add when overflow is expected.

cards.q: What does a function return if the last line of its body is `x * x;` with a semicolon?
cards.a:
`()` (unit), which is a type error if the function declares `-> i32`

The semicolon turns the expression into a statement, so the body's value becomes `()`; the compiler then suggests removing the semicolon.

cards.q: Can `if` be used on the right of a `let`?
cards.a:
Yes: `if` is an expression, as long as both branches give the same type

`let s = if c { a } else { b };` works because `if` produces a value; the variable needs one type, so both branches must agree.

cards.q: What is the value of `{ let a = 2; a * 3 }`?
cards.a:
6

The block's value is its last expression, `a * 3`, which has no semicolon.

cards.q: How can a `loop` produce a value?
cards.a:
With `break value;`, which makes the `loop` expression evaluate to `value`

`break value;` gives the whole `loop` expression that value, as in `let result = loop { ... };`. `return` would leave the whole function instead.

cards.q: Which numbers does the range `1..=5` include?
cards.a:
1, 2, 3, 4 and 5

`..=` includes the end; `1..5` would stop at 4.

cards.q: A `match` on an `i32` lists arms for 0 and 1 only. What happens?
cards.a:
It does not compile: the patterns are not exhaustive

`match` must cover every possible value; add a `_` arm for the rest.

cards.q: Which parameter type should a function that only reads text use?
cards.a:
`&str`

`&str` accepts string literals and borrowed `String`s alike. `String` would take the caller's string away, and `&String` would not accept a literal.

cards.q: Why must you trim the result of `read_line` before parsing it?
cards.a:
`read_line` keeps the line break, and `"42\n"` does not parse as a number

The line break typed by the user stays at the end of the string; `trim()` removes it (and any spaces) before `parse`.

cards.q: What does `"5x".parse::<i32>()` give?
cards.a:
An `Err` value

`parse` returns a `Result`; it only panics if you `unwrap` the `Err`.

cards.q: When is a `String`'s heap memory freed?
cards.a:
When its owner goes out of scope, unless it was moved elsewhere first

The owner drops the value at the end of its scope; if ownership moved (to another variable or a function), the new owner frees it instead. Rust has no garbage collector.

cards.q: Why can you still use `a` after `let b = a;` when `a` is an `i32` but not when it is a `String`?
cards.a:
`i32` is `Copy`, so it is copied; a `String` owns heap data, so it is moved

Copying an `i32` is trivial and safe; two owners of one `String` buffer would both free it, so the `String` moves and `a` becomes unusable. A deep copy needs an explicit `.clone()`.

cards.q: After `let v = vec![1, 2]; let w = v;`, which is true?
cards.a:
The vector moved to `w` and `v` can no longer be used

`Vec` owns heap memory, so assignment moves it; the code compiles as long as `v` is not used afterwards.

cards.q: Why can't you hold `&v[0]` while calling `v.push(4)`?
cards.a:
`push` may move the buffer, leaving the reference pointing at freed memory

`push` needs a mutable borrow, which is not allowed while a shared borrow is alive; that rule stops the reference from dangling when the buffer is reallocated.

cards.q: How do you add 1 to the `i32` behind an `&mut i32` parameter `n`?
cards.a:
`*n += 1;`

`n` is a reference; `*n` dereferences it to reach the `i32` it points to.

cards.q: Which combination of borrows of one value can exist at the same time?
cards.a:
Three shared references

Many readers or one writer, never both.

cards.q: Why should a function that sums numbers take `&[i32]` instead of `&Vec<i32>`?
cards.a:
A slice also accepts arrays and parts of vectors, not only whole vectors

`&[i32]` works for `&array`, `&vector` and `&vector[1..3]`; `&Vec<i32>` only for a whole vector. Neither one moves the data.

cards.q: What does `&s[0..3]` contain for `s = "hello"`?
cards.a:
"hel"

The range takes bytes 0, 1 and 2: the end index is not included.

cards.q: What does `[1, 2, 3, 4].windows(2).count()` return?
cards.a:
3

`windows(2)` yields the overlapping pairs [1, 2], [2, 3] and [3, 4]; `chunks(2)` would give 2.

cards.q: What is the difference between `&self` and `&mut self` in a method?
cards.a:
`&self` borrows the value to read it; `&mut self` borrows it so fields can change

Both are borrows: `&self` is a shared borrow for reading, `&mut self` a mutable one for updating fields. Taking ownership is plain `self`.

cards.q: How is an associated function such as `new` called?
cards.a:
With the type name and `::`, as in `Counter::new("clicks")`

An associated function has no `self` parameter, so there is no value to call it on; Rust has no `new` keyword.

cards.q: A method takes `self` (not a reference). What happens to the value it is called on?
cards.a:
It is moved into the method and cannot be used afterwards, unless it is `Copy`

`self` takes ownership, like passing the value to any function.

cards.q: Why is `Option<T>` safer than null?
cards.a:
The type says the value may be missing, and you must handle `None` to use it

The compiler will not let you use the `T` inside without dealing with the `None` case (by `match`, `if let`, `unwrap_or`, ...), so a forgotten check cannot compile.

cards.q: What does `?` do on an `Option` inside a function that returns `Option`?
cards.a:
It unwraps `Some(v)` to `v`, or returns `None` from the function at once

`?` is an early return for the `None` case; panicking is what `unwrap()` does.

cards.q: What is `Some(4).map(|x| x * 2).filter(|x| *x > 10).unwrap_or(0)`?
cards.a:
0

`map` gives `Some(8)`, the filter rejects it (8 is not above 10), and `unwrap_or` supplies 0.

cards.q: What is the difference between `v[5]` and `v.get(5)` when `v` has 3 items?
cards.a:
`v[5]` panics; `v.get(5)` gives `None`

Indexing panics when the index is out of range (the compiler cannot know the length); `get` returns an `Option` instead.

cards.q: What happens to a vector `v` after `for x in v { }`?
cards.a:
It is moved into the loop and consumed; loop over `&v` to keep it

Looping over `v` by value moves it, even when the items are `Copy`; `for x in &v` borrows instead.

cards.q: What is `v` after `let mut v = vec![1, 1, 2, 1]; v.dedup();`?
cards.a:
[1, 2, 1]

`dedup` only removes consecutive duplicates; sort first to remove all repeats.

cards.q: Why does `"é".len()` return 2?
cards.a:
`len` counts bytes, and `é` takes two bytes in UTF-8

A `String` is UTF-8: ASCII takes one byte, `é` two, and others up to four. `s.chars().count()` counts characters.

cards.q: How do you get each character together with the byte position where it starts?
cards.a:
`s.char_indices()`

`char_indices()` gives (byte position, char) pairs. `chars().enumerate()` counts characters, so its numbers are wrong for slicing once a multi-byte character appears.

cards.q: Which is a valid way to get the first character of a `String` `s`?
cards.a:
`s.chars().next()`

Strings are not indexable by position; `chars()` goes through the characters, and `next()` gives the first (an `Option<char>`).

cards.q: What does `*counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1` do?
cards.a:
Inserts 0 for a new word, then adds 1 to the stored count either way

`or_insert(0)` returns a `&mut` to the stored count (inserting 0 first if the word is new), and `*... += 1` increments it.

cards.q: When should you choose `BTreeMap` over `HashMap`?
cards.a:
When you need the keys kept in sorted order

`BTreeMap` keeps keys sorted (O(log n) operations), which also gives key ranges and the smallest or largest key; `HashMap` is faster on average but iterates in no particular order. Neither accepts `f64` keys.

cards.q: What does `HashSet::insert` return when the value is already in the set?
cards.a:
false

`insert` returns whether the value was newly added.

cards.q: What does the `?` operator do with an `Err` value?
cards.a:
It returns the error from the current function at once (via `From` if needed)

`?` is early-return plumbing: `Ok(v)` becomes `v`, and `Err(e)` is returned to the caller. Panicking is what `unwrap()` does.

cards.q: When is panicking the right choice instead of returning a `Result`?
cards.a:
For bugs and broken invariants that the caller cannot sensibly handle

Bad input and missing files are expected failures the caller can handle, so they deserve a `Result`; a panic is for "this should be impossible".

cards.q: What is `"7".parse::<i32>().map(|n| n * 2).unwrap_or(0)`?
cards.a:
14

`parse` gives `Ok(7)`, `map` doubles it, and `unwrap_or` takes the value out of the `Ok`.

cards.q: Can code outside a module call a function in it that is not marked `pub`?
cards.a:
No: items are private to their module and its children unless marked `pub`

Privacy applies whatever the path: `geometry::square(2.0)` is refused because `square` is not `pub`.

cards.q: Why do unit tests live in a `mod tests` with `#[cfg(test)]`?
cards.a:
It is compiled only for `cargo test`, and as a child module it can reach private items

`#[cfg(test)]` leaves the module out of normal builds, and `use super::*;` gives it the parent's items, private ones included.

cards.q: A `pub struct Account` has a private field `balance`. What can code in another module do?
cards.a:
Only use it through its public functions and methods

Private fields are invisible outside the module, so other code cannot even build an `Account` with a struct literal: construction must go through a public function such as `new`.

cards.q: Why does `fn largest<T>(items: &[T]) -> T` need a bound such as `PartialOrd`?
cards.a:
Without it the compiler knows nothing about `T`, so `>` is not allowed

The body is checked once for every possible `T`; only what the bounds promise (here, comparing with `>`) may be used.

cards.q: What does `impl Pair<f64> { ... }` mean?
cards.a:
Those methods exist only for `Pair<f64>`, not for other `Pair` types

An `impl` for one concrete type adds methods just to that type; `impl<T> Pair<T>` would cover every `Pair`.

cards.q: What does monomorphization mean for generic code?
cards.a:
The compiler makes a specialised copy for each type used, with no run-time cost

Each use with a concrete type is compiled as if written by hand for it; the price is compile time and binary size.

cards.q: What is a default method in a trait?
cards.a:
A method with a body in the trait, which implementers get for free and may override

`describe` in `Shape` is a default method: `Circle` keeps it, while `Rect` overrides it with its own version.

cards.q: Why can't you implement `std::fmt::Display` for `Vec<i32>`?
cards.a:
The orphan rule: neither the trait nor the type is defined in your crate

You may implement a trait for a type only if one of them is yours; wrap the `Vec` in your own struct (a newtype) instead.

cards.q: A function takes `items: &[S]` with `S: Shape`. Can it receive a mix of circles and squares?
cards.a:
No: `S` is one type per call; mixing needs `dyn Shape` trait objects

A generic parameter is filled in with a single type for each call; `&[Box<dyn Shape>]` can hold different shapes.

cards.q: Why can't `f64` implement `Eq` and `Ord`?
cards.a:
`NaN` is not equal to itself and has no order, so both are only partial

`Eq` promises every value equals itself and `Ord` that any two values are ordered; `NaN` breaks both, so `f64` only has `PartialEq` and `PartialOrd`.

cards.q: What do you get for free by implementing `From<A> for B`?
cards.a:
`Into<B>` for `A`, so `a.into()` produces a `B`

The standard library implements `Into` for every `From`, which is why you implement `From` and never `Into` directly. Nothing gives you the reverse conversion.

cards.q: Two `#[derive(PartialOrd)]` structs are compared. How is the order decided?
cards.a:
Field by field, in declaration order

Derived comparisons are lexicographic: the first field that differs decides, in declaration order, so `major` decides before `minor`.

cards.q: What does `fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str` promise?
cards.a:
The result is valid while both inputs are, so it may borrow from either

One lifetime for all three means the result can only be used while both inputs are still alive: the shorter of the two lifetimes.

cards.q: Why does `fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str` need no lifetime annotation?
cards.a:
With one input reference, elision gives the output that same lifetime

The elision rules fill in `fn first_word<'a>(s: &'a str) -> &'a str`. With two input references, like `longest`, you must write them.

cards.q: What is the type of the literal `"hello"`?
cards.a:
&'static str

Literals are stored in the program binary and live for the whole run.

cards.q: Why must a `dyn Trait` value sit behind a pointer such as `Box` or `&`?
cards.a:
Its concrete type, and so its size, is not known at compile time

A variable needs a size fixed at compile time; a pointer has one, whatever type it points to. `&dyn Shape` works too, so the heap is not required.

cards.q: When is an enum better than `Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`?
cards.a:
When the set of types is fixed: `match` is checked for completeness, with no vtable

A closed set suits an enum; trait objects suit an open set that other code may extend. Both can hold variants with different data.

cards.q: Which trait method makes a trait unusable as `dyn Trait`?
cards.a:
`fn duplicate(&self) -> Self`

Returning `Self` needs the concrete type's size, which a trait object hides.

cards.q: What does writing `move` in front of a closure change?
cards.a:
It captures the variables it uses by value, taking ownership of them

`move` changes how variables are captured (by value instead of by reference). It does not make a closure `FnOnce`: a `move` closure that only reads its captures is still `Fn`.

cards.q: A function calls the closure it receives many times, and the closure may change its captures. Which bound should it use?
cards.a:
`FnMut`

`FnMut` allows changing captures and calling many times (one at a time). `Fn` would reject closures that change state, and `FnOnce` allows only one call.

cards.q: A closure moves a captured String out (returns it). Which traits does it implement?
cards.a:
FnOnce only

Giving away a captured value can only happen once, so the closure is only `FnOnce`.

cards.q: Why does `(1..).map(|n| n * n).filter(|n| n % 3 == 1)` not run forever?
cards.a:
Adapters are lazy: nothing is computed until a consumer asks for values

Building the chain does no work. Only a consumer such as `take(5).collect()` pulls values through, and it stops asking after five.

cards.q: What does collecting an iterator of `Result<T, E>` into `Result<Vec<T>, E>` do?
cards.a:
Gives `Ok` with all the values, or the first `Err`, stopping there

The errors are not skipped: one `Err` makes the whole result that `Err`, and collecting stops at it.

cards.q: What must you write to implement `Iterator` for your own type?
cards.a:
The associated type `Item` and the method `next`

You choose `type Item` and write `next`; every other iterator method (`map`, `filter`, `sum`...) is provided for free.

cards.q: Why does `Words<'a>` need a lifetime parameter?
cards.a:
Its items borrow from the original text, which must outlive them

`Words` holds a `&str` and hands out `&'a str` slices of it, so the compiler must know how long that text lives. `Countdown` has no references and needs no lifetime.

cards.q: How many items does `Countdown { current: 3 }` produce?
cards.a:
3

It yields 3, 2 and 1, then returns None.

cards.q: Why does a recursive enum like `List` need a `Box`?
cards.a:
Without a pointer the type would contain itself and have infinite size

A `Box` has the fixed size of a pointer, so `Cons(i32, Box<List>)` has a known size. Sharing a tail between owners is what `Rc` is for.

cards.q: What happens if you call `borrow_mut()` on a `RefCell` that is already borrowed?
cards.a:
It panics at run time

`RefCell` checks the borrowing rules while the program runs, so breaking them is a panic, not a compile error.

cards.q: What does `Rc::clone(&a)` copy?
cards.a:
Only the pointer, incrementing the reference count

Rc::clone is cheap: it shares the same allocation.

cards.q: What does `c @ 'a'..='z'` do in a match arm?
cards.a:
Matches a char in that range and binds the matched value to `c`

`name @ pattern` tests the pattern and, if it matches, binds the whole matched value to the name.

cards.q: Why can't you write `let Some(x) = maybe_value;` without `else`?
cards.a:
`Some(x)` is refutable: `let` needs a pattern that always matches, or an `else`

A refutable pattern can fail to match, so plain `let` rejects it at compile time. `let ... else` says what to do when it does not match.

cards.q: Which pattern matches a slice with at least two items and binds the first and last?
cards.a:
[first, .., last]

.. in a slice pattern matches any number of items in the middle, including none.

cards.q: Why does `thread::spawn` usually need a `move` closure?
cards.a:
The thread may outlive the function, so it must own its data instead of borrowing it

A spawned thread can keep running after the function that started it returns, so borrowing its locals is refused. `thread::scope` is the way to let threads borrow.

cards.q: When does a `for` loop over an `mpsc` receiver end?
cards.a:
When every sender has been dropped and the channel is empty

An empty channel only makes the receiver wait. The loop ends once no sender is left, which is why the example drops the original `tx`.

cards.q: Why can't an `Rc<T>` be sent to another thread?
cards.a:
Its count is not updated atomically, so it is not `Send`

Two threads changing the count at once could corrupt it. `Arc` is the thread-safe version with an atomic count.

cards.q: Why does a Rust `Mutex` hold the data inside it rather than sit next to it?
cards.a:
So the only way to reach the data is through `lock()`

With the data inside, forgetting to lock is impossible to write: the guard from `lock()` is the only way in.
cards.lessonTitle: Shared State with Arc and Mutex

cards.q: What is the thread-safe counterpart of `Rc<RefCell<T>>`?
cards.a:
`Arc<Mutex<T>>`

`Arc` replaces `Rc` for shared ownership across threads and `Mutex` (or `RwLock`) replaces `RefCell` for changing the data. `Rc` is not `Send` and `RefCell` is not `Sync`.
cards.lessonTitle: Shared State with Arc and Mutex

cards.q: When is a Mutex's lock released?
cards.a:
When the guard returned by lock() is dropped

The guard releases the lock in its Drop implementation, typically at the end of the statement or block.
cards.lessonTitle: Shared State with Arc and Mutex

cards.q: What does calling an `async fn` return?
cards.a:
A future, which does nothing until it is awaited or spawned

Futures are lazy: calling the function only builds the future, and a runtime drives it when you `.await` or spawn it.

cards.q: Why is calling `std::thread::sleep` inside an async task a problem?
cards.a:
It blocks the runtime's thread, stopping the other tasks on it

It compiles, but it blocks the whole thread, so no other task on that thread can run. Use `tokio::time::sleep(...).await` instead.

cards.q: Two futures each wait 1 second. How long does `tokio::join!(a, b)` take?
cards.a:
About 1 second

join! runs both concurrently and finishes when both are done.

cards.q: What are documentation tests?
cards.a:
Code examples in `///` comments that `cargo test` compiles and runs

Because the examples in the docs are compiled and run, they cannot silently go stale.

cards.q: Why measure performance only with `--release` builds?
cards.a:
Debug builds are unoptimised and add checks, so they can be much slower

Debug builds skip optimisation and keep checks such as overflow panics, so their timings say little about the real program.

cards.q: Where do integration tests live in a Cargo project?
cards.a:
In the tests/ folder next to src/

Each file in tests/ is compiled as its own crate that uses only the public API.

cards.q: Why should `main` stay small in a command-line program?
cards.a:
The logic then sits in testable functions, and only `main` reports errors

Functions that take text and return a `Result` are easy to unit test; `main` alone decides what to print and which exit code to use.

cards.q: Why read standard input when no file path is given?
cards.a:
The tool can then sit in a pipeline, reading another program's output

With standard input, `cat app.log | logsum --level error` works. Reading stdin can still fail, so it still returns a `Result`.

cards.q: What should a command-line tool do when it fails?
cards.a:
Print the error to standard error and exit with a non-zero code

Scripts check the exit code, and errors on stderr do not mix with the real output.

cards.q: Why does `square!(2 + 3)` give 25 rather than 11?
cards.a:
The `expr` fragment keeps `2 + 3` as one unit, like `(2 + 3) * (2 + 3)`

A macro expands into code rather than calling anything, but an `expr` fragment stays one expression; plain text substitution would give `2 + 3 * 2 + 3`, which is 11.

cards.q: What does `$( ... ),*` mean in a macro pattern?
cards.a:
The part in brackets may appear any number of times, separated by commas

`*` means zero or more repetitions with the separator between them; `+` would mean one or more, and `$(,)?` is the optional trailing comma.

cards.q: Which fragment specifier would capture the name of a struct to be defined?
cards.a:
ident

An ident is a name; it can be used to declare a new item.

cards.q: Why take `&str` rather than `&String` as a parameter?
cards.a:
Deref coercion turns `&String` into `&str`, so `&str` accepts every kind of string

`&String`, `&Box<String>` and literals all become `&str`, while a `&String` parameter accepts only `&String`. Neither kind owns, copies or changes the text.

cards.q: When does `Cow` save work?
cards.a:
When the function usually returns its input unchanged

In the common case it hands back the borrowed input (`Cow::Borrowed`) instead of allocating a copy; only the rare changed case pays for a `String`.

cards.q: Which trait lets HashMap<String, i32>::get accept a &str?
cards.a:
Borrow

String implements Borrow<str>, and get takes any borrowed form of the key.

cards.q: Does `unsafe` turn off the borrow checker?
cards.a:
No: it allows five extra operations, and all other checks stay on

The borrow checker, type checks and bounds checks still apply inside `unsafe`; the block only unlocks operations such as dereferencing raw pointers.

cards.q: Why is calling a C function always unsafe?
cards.a:
The compiler cannot see inside it to check that it is memory-safe

Rust cannot check what foreign code does, so the caller must promise that the call is correct, even for something as harmless as `abs`.

cards.q: Which of these needs an unsafe block?
cards.a:
reading the value a raw pointer points to

Making a raw pointer is safe; dereferencing it is one of the five unsafe operations.

cards.q: When should you use a `BufReader` instead of `read_to_string`?
cards.a:
When the file may be large, so it is read a piece at a time

`read_to_string` loads the whole file into memory; `BufReader` with `lines()` keeps only a little of it at once. Binary data is what `fs::read` is for.

cards.q: Why pass the arguments to `Command` as a list?
cards.a:
Each argument stays one argument, whatever characters it contains

Nothing is interpreted by a shell, so a file name with spaces or quotes cannot split into several arguments or break the command.

cards.q: What does Path::new("a/b/report.txt").extension() return?
cards.a:
Some("txt")

extension gives the part after the last dot, without the dot, as an Option.

cards.q: Why do the transition methods such as `review` take `self` and not `&mut self`?
cards.a:
Taking ownership moves the value, so the old state cannot be used again

After `post.review()`, `post` has been moved and any later `post.edit(...)` fails to compile. With `&mut self`, the draft would still be usable.

cards.q: What does a `PhantomData<T>` field cost at run time?
cards.a:
Nothing: it has size zero

It only tells the compiler that the type uses `T`; `Id<Order>` is still just 4 bytes, the size of its `u32`.

cards.q: fn charge(id: Id<User>) is called with an Id<Order>. What happens?
cards.a:
a compile error: the types differ

Id<User> and Id<Order> are different types, which is the whole point.

cards.q: What does `?` do with an error before returning it?
cards.a:
It calls `From::from` to convert it into the function's error type

That conversion is why implementing `From<ParseIntError> for AppError` lets a plain `text.parse()?` work in a function returning `Result<_, AppError>`.

cards.q: When is `Box<dyn Error>` a good choice?
cards.a:
In applications or small programs that only report errors

A boxed error can hold any error type but cannot be matched by variant, so libraries should give callers their own error enum instead.

cards.q: What should source() return for an error that wraps an io::Error?
cards.a:
Some(the wrapped io::Error)

`source()` gives access to the underlying error, so the cause can be shown or inspected; following `source()` again and again walks the chain of causes.

cards.q: Why implement `From` rather than `Into`?
cards.a:
Implementing `From<A> for B` gives you `Into<B> for A` automatically

With one `From` impl you get both `B::from(a)` and `a.into()`, so there is nothing to gain by writing `Into` by hand.

cards.q: What is wrong with `x as u8` for an `i32` that may be large?
cards.a:
It silently wraps (300 becomes 44) instead of reporting a problem

`as` keeps only the low 8 bits without any error; `u8::try_from(x)` returns an `Err` for values that do not fit.

cards.q: Which trait makes "1,2".parse::<Point>() possible?
cards.a:
FromStr for Point

str::parse calls the type's FromStr implementation.

cards.q: Why does `dedup` on `vec![1, 2, 1]` leave all three items?
cards.a:
It only removes equal items that are next to each other

The two `1`s are not neighbours, so nothing is removed. Sort first to remove every duplicate.

cards.q: How do you make a `BinaryHeap` give the smallest item first?
cards.a:
Push the values wrapped in `std::cmp::Reverse`

A `BinaryHeap` always gives its largest item; `Reverse` flips the comparison, so the smallest value counts as the largest.

cards.q: [2, 5, 8].binary_search(&6) gives...
cards.a:
Err(2)

6 is not there, so the result is `Err` with the place where it would be inserted: index 2, between 5 and 8.

cards.q: When should a trait use an associated type instead of a generic parameter?
cards.a:
When each implementing type has exactly one natural choice, like an iterator's item

With an associated type there is one `Item` per implementation, so calls need no annotation. Implementing a trait several times for one type is what a generic parameter (`Container<T>`) allows.

cards.q: What does `impl<T: Display> Shout for T` do?
cards.a:
It implements `Shout` for every type that implements `Display`, all at once

That is a blanket implementation, like `impl<T: Display> ToString for T`. Requiring `Display` for every `Shout` type would be a supertrait (`trait Shout: Display`).

cards.q: What must a type implement for iter.sum::<T>() to work?
cards.a:
Sum

Iterator::sum is defined for any S: Sum<Self::Item>; Add alone is not enough.

cards.q: Why does `term` handle `*` while `expr` handles `+`?
cards.a:
`expr` calls `term` for its parts, so multiplications are grouped first

The nesting of the functions is the precedence: each part of a sum is a whole product. Grouping from the left comes from the loop in `expr`.

cards.q: Why keep the position of each token?
cards.a:
So error messages can say where the problem is

With positions, an error can point at the column, which helps users more than anything else a parser does.

cards.q: In recursive descent, how does a grammar rule become code?
cards.a:
as a function that calls the functions of the rules it uses

Each rule is a function; using another rule means calling its function, so nesting in the grammar becomes recursion.
